### **1.  Introduction & Executive Summary** 

#### **1.1 Introduction** 

In our previous Quarterly Three Year Copper Forecast, we suggested that the elevated level of prices, which saw the cash quote average $9,646/tonne in the first quarter, would be unsustainable in the short term. Although the turning point in prices came slightly later than we had initially envisaged, this proved to be the case.  Despite copper’s superior fundamentals compared to most of the rest of the base sector, the metal has not been immune to the recent concerns about the global economy with the second quarter average coming in just over 5% lower at $9,137/tonne. However, the weakness was relatively limited and over the June to August period the monthly average price was above $9,000/tonne, compared to the low for the year of $8,537/tonne recorded in mid-May. 

In terms of daily prices, the high for the year was recorded in mid-February at $10,148/tonne.  It should be noted that the copper market has struggled to maintain a level of above $10,000/tonne for any sustained period of time; a trend we expect to continue.  The difference between this high and the aforementioned low for the year, of under 20%, was the lowest within the base metals complex.  This reflects in part that any dips in the copper price are generally seen as buying opportunities.  This view is not just restricted to the more speculative elements of the market such as investment funds, with Thomson Reuters GFMS noting good buying by consumers and physical traders 

on any price weakness.  The copper market has largely weathered recent concerns about the global economy and prices in early September were hovering around $9,000/tonne. 

The other way to measure copper’s performance is to compare the price of copper with the rest of the base metals.  Thomson Reuters GFMS’ preferred approach is to use a basket of LME prices applying an equal weighting to all the base metals.  This compares to the LME’s own index which is heavily weighted towards the two largest metals, aluminium (41.8%) and copper (33.4%).  The average copper price in the first eight months of this year was up 24%, while the broader index was just 14% higher. 

The fundamentals have provided underlying support to the market, with production continuing to underperform expectations and underlying demand, particularly in the developing economies, remaining robust. Consequently, Thomson Reuters GFMS estimates that the market was in deficit in first half of 2011.  However, statistical discrepancies mean that this has not necessarily been reflected in reported stock movements so far this year.  Up to the end of August, terminal market stocks have increased by close to 100,000 tonnes. Trends with the Chinese market continue to mask the underlying figures as the process of stock reduction of unreported inventories that were built up in 2009 and early 2010 is still ongoing. Indeed, tighter credit conditions within China have seen some of this material return to the market, resulting in a massive discrepancy between apparent consumption statistics and Thomson Reuters GFMS’ estimates of underlying Chinese consumption (see Chapter 3 for more details). Importantly, we continue to note robust growth in the copper fabricating sector and the industries it serves, and expect Chinese demand to grow by around 6.8% this year. #### **1.2 Economic Assumptions** Since our last report, concerns over the debt problem in both Europe and the United States have taken centre stage. The debt ‘contagion’ is not limited to Europe alone with problems in the United States resulting in a downgrade in its AAA debt rating. Furthermore, the escalation of the sovereign debt crisis has also raised worries regarding a potential slowdown in the world economy. Already in the past few months, there is increasing evidence that GDP growth in a number of advanced economies has dropped considerably. Trends in the OECD composite leading indicator have also been far from encouraging, with the indicator falling for five months in a row to 101.6 in July. Even in emerging markets where growth has been fairly strong, continuing inflationary pressures on the back of a sharp rally in commodity prices has prompted authorities in a number of countries to tighten monetary policy further, also slowing the global economy. **Base Case Scenario** (with a 45% probability outcome): Our forecast for global economic growth in 2011 has been rev

ised lower since our last report. 

After a major rebound in 2010, world GDP growth is set to slow down this year to 2.7%.  This is due to the indebted nature of both governments and consumers in much of the developed world.  Meanwhile, further tightening of monetary policies in emerging markets to fight surging inflation will also slow down world GDP growth this year.  This is followed by marginally faster growth over the remainder of the forecast period as the more traditional sources of growth, such as consumer spending and the property market, start to improve. The latter will be aided by unemployment beginning to slowly recede, albeit from elevated levels. 

US GDP grew at an annualised rate of 1.3% in the second quarter, well below the consensus range.  The main reason for these disappointing figures was weak consumer spending, as this key driver of the US economy rose by a mere 0.1% from April to June this year.  Meanwhile, it also reflects a continuation of an elevated unemployment rate coupled with a lacklustre property market, both of which are likely to remain in place for an extended period.  This combined with the waning support from fiscal policy will certainly restrict annual GDP growth to an annual average of just over 2.0% over the final three years of our forecast period. 

Given the extensive problems across the EU-27, we expect GDP growth in the region this year to be restricted to 1.3%.  Ominously, growth in Germany and France, the two largest economies in Europe, both stalled in the second quarter.  Given the excessive level of public debt in many European countries, we would expect further austerity measures to take place over the coming years.  As such, we continue to expect only modest GDP growth over the forecast period as its economies gradually recover.

Japan’s economy has recovered faster than expected from the aftermath of the earthquake and tsunami. However a number of other factors remain a threat, particularly in terms of a stronger Japanese yen; due to the ongoing debt issues in the United States and Europe, the yen rose to record highs against the dollar in late July, which put further pressure on the export sector.  Next year, given more pipeline increases together with further construction in the earthquakedamaged regions, the economy is expected to rebound by 2.0%. 

China’s economic growth has slowed further in the second quarter after the government stepped up its battle against surging inflation, which rose to a three-year-high of 6.5% in July.  Looking ahead, the government will still treat managing inflation as the priority in the near term, with more interest rate hikes likely to take place over the rest of the year. Nevertheless, China is unlikely to see a hard landing, as the economy should benefit from continued policy efforts to raise disposable incomes, with the drivers of growth shifting increasingly from the public to the priv

ate sector. We therefore forecast China’s economy to expand at least 9.0% this year. Moving to 2012, despite a continuation of a tighter monetary policy, growth is likely to remain solid and stable, albeit at a slightly slower pace of 8.5%. Accordingly, many advanced economies border on very low levels of inflation. Therefore, global GDP growth is a poor 2.1% this year, with developed economies massively underperforming even that meagre result. In 2012 and further still in 2013, growth rates improve but remain at historically low levels, especially for a post-recession phase of economic growth. A key factor behind these sluggish growth rates is the high level of indebtedness of governments in developed economies, including the world’s largest single economy, the United States, where, as a result, fiscal tightening also eventually takes place. As a consequence, that country sees just 1.0% growth in 2011 as the economy stagnates and the ongoing loose monetary policy is ineffective in ensuring economic recovery continues at the former pace. Given the industrialisation taking place in many developing countries they will continue to be the best performers. Needless to say Chinese growth will be the strongest among the larger countries in this group, although by its standards an increase of 8.1% this year would represent a fair dip. India’s growth rate is also expected to hold up well, with an average rate of 6.6% over the forecast period. #### **1.3 The D

ollar** 

The US dollar has remained generally weak since the release of our previous forecast, with the greenback averaging $1.43/€ in June and July.  A key reason for this is market expectations that monetary policy will remain extremely loose, particularly compared with the European Central Bank who delivered its second interest rate rise in July in an attempt to fight inflation. In contrast, the latest comment from Bernake indicated that the Federal Reserve is ready to start QE3 if the economy continues to worsen.  In fact, until there is credible evidence that the Fed is likely to raise interest rates in the near term, the dollar is likely to remain

under pressure.  As such, we expect the dollar:euro rate to rise to an average of $1.40/€ this year. 

Nevertheless, mainly based on its current purchasing power parity (PPP) undervaluation, we would expect the US dollar to strengthen against the euro in the latter part of the forecast period.  Consequently, we forecast a secular appreciation in the US dollar (against most currencies) under our Base Case from 2012 onwards.  Besides the convergence towards long run PPP referred to above, this move will be assisted by the fact that by then the Federal Reserve will, finally, start to raise interest rates from their current exceptionally low levels.  We therefore expect the US dollar to average $1.38/€ in 2012 and $1.35/€ in 2013, before weakening further to $1.27/€ in the final year of our forecast period. 

#### **1.4 Investment** 

Investment activity continues to exert a significant impact on pricing.  For the bulk of this year this has been a supportive factor.  Even against a background of increasing uncertainty in the economic climate there has not been a mass exodus from the sector. Unfortunately there is limited publically available information on investment activity in the copper market.  We track the speculative positions in Comex futures, which is published by the CFTC.  Essentially the net long position has declined from the highs seen earlier this year and in early September the net long position was 32,676 lots (370,540 tonnes) compared to 73,328 lots (831,526 tonnes) on 4th January. 

Copper generally attracts greater volumes of investment interest than the other base metals.  Given this background one might expect that copper would suffer the most as sentiment turns negative towards industrial commodities as concerns about economic growth increase.  However copper has outperformed its peers in recent months.  This seeming contradiction is due to copper’s superior fundamentals.  Investment funds are by no means a homogeneous group.  They range from technical funds to macro and commodity specific funds, with the latter in particular focusing on the fundamentals. 

We also note that within the commodity investments universe there has been a gradual shift of investors’ attention to managed strategies.  In pa

rt, this is due to the disappointment of index funds underperforming their benchmark. Also, as investors have grown more accustomed to investment in the commodity sector, there is greater focus on the commodities with the perceived better fundamentals and copper has been a beneficiary of this trend. While investment activity has been broadly supportive to the copper market it should be remembered that all asset classes go in and out of favour with the postLehman collapse in copper prices reinforcing this point. Our base case for the economic outlook is that growth will not be derailed by the current problems. As such, we expect that funds will largely maintain a long side bias. **6** 3-Year Copper Forecast - September 2011 **CONFIDENTIAL** #### **1.5 Consumption** Thomson Reuters GFMS’ Copper Survey 2011 highlights detailed end-use and regional trends for the copper industry. Broken down by sector, the data shows that electrical and electronic products remained the largest market in 2010 with a 37% share. The construction market accounted for 31% of the total, down from 32% in the previous year, primarily due to the ongoing weakness of this sector within the mature economies. Elsewhere, the transportation and consumer and general products sectors gained market share, buoyed by stimulus measures and the release of pent-up demand, and both accounted for 11% of total demand. Finally, the industrial machinery sector accounted for around 10% of the global total. Global copper consumption registered a strong recovery in 2010, rising 11.1% year-on-year to 19.289 million tonnes, which was well in excess of the levels seen prior to the financial crisis. This strength has, however, somewhat softened over the first half of 2011, mainly in line with the uncertain nature of the economic recovery and the absence of the pipeline restocking process that supported the rebound in demand growth seen last year. The growth of copper usage in the mature economies is expected to slow over the forecast period, in part due to ongoing substitution and miniaturisation pressures. By the latter year of our forecast period, Thomson

Reuters GFMS expect growth amongst the group to total just 0.2%. The emerging markets have continued to grow robustly in tonnage terms so far this year, with a notable increase in Russian consumption driving up the regional total (see Chapter 3 for details). Elsewhere within the group, although significant in tonnage terms, the increases have however generally moderated from the rapid rate of expansion seen over previous years. This, to a large extent, has been a response to the moderation in economic growth and the tightening of monetary policies implemented in these countries. In focusing on the largest copper consumer, China, we are however optimistic on the demand outlook. Indeed, although China’s government has adopted tight monetary policies in an effort to combat high inflation, copper consumption should continue to grow at a robust rate given the significant number of scheduled infrastructure-related projects. Over the forecast period, Thomson Reuters GFMS expect the BRICs’ consumption to grow at an average annual rate of 6.7%. Given the slowdown in copper consumption growth in both the mature and emerging economies, Thomson Reuters GFMS forecast the growth in global demand to slow to 5.4% this year, with the total standing at 20.321 million tonnes. Similar themes are expected to limit the growth in consumption over 2012 to 3.8%. Thereafter, intensifying trends towards substitution and miniaturisation are set to impose further downside over 2013 and 2014 (together with the potential for a cyclical slowdown towards the end of the forecast period), when consumption growth is expected to moderate to 3.5%, and 3.3% respectively, with the global total reaching 22.554 million tonnes in the latter year. **7** 3-Year Copper Forecast - September 2011 **CONFIDENTIAL** #### **1.6 Production** In our last Quarterly report, Thomson Reuters GFMS expected the high copper prices to encourage an acceleration in refined production. However, with mine supply having continued to be affected by a combination of labour disputes, weather-related disruptions and technical problems, growth in primary output has once again come in below expectations. A key impetus to the positive growth in refined output so far this year has thus been higher scrap supply, which has been fuelled by

the relatively high price environment. We expect the latter to be boosted by the fact that, according to anecdotal evidence, scrap stockpiles have not yet been quite depleted. This coupled with a modest increase in mine output should see global refined output increase by 4% to 19.851 million tonnes this year. Going forward, we expect stronger increases in mine production over 2012-2014. We expect that secondary production growth will be faster than mine supply overall although at a slightly slower rate than in 20102011. As a result, refined production growth should stand above 4% in all three years. As we move into 2012, despite a number of projects being pushed back by a year or so over the forecast period, we expect global production growth to accelerate. Output next year is expected to increase by 4.1%, in part reflecting an increase at the huge Grasberg mine in Indonesia and additional capacity most notably in Africa and the Americas. This, coupled with accelerating growth in Europe, should see global mine production reach just under 17.1 million tonnes next year. In the final two years of the forecast period, we expect production growth of 4.9% and 5.6%, respectively, bringing the total to 18.912 million tonnes, 15.3% up on this year’s estimate of 16.405 million tonnes. Implicit in these two years is the fact that some of the projects that we expected would come on stream by the end of 2011 and in 2012 will be realised in be final two years of our forecast. By this time, we expect decelerating growth in Asia and Africa to be offset by rising growth in the Americas. #### **1.7 Market Outlook** #### Base Case Scenario The tightness at the concentrate stage has continued to persist. This, combined with lower than expected output from SX-EW operations, in part due to technical problems, has seen global mine production grow by just over 2% over the first five months of the year. As a result, Thomson Reuters GFMS are forecasting global mine production to grow by just 3% this year, slightly down on our previous forecast of 3.5%. As discussed earlier, despite copper’s superior fundamentals compared to the rest of the base metals, the market has not been immune to the weakness that has affected the broader LME complex and the financial markets. Our analysis of the underlying market fundamentals is largely unchanged in that we still see the market in a structural deficit i.e. producers are struggling to raise 

output in response to high price levels.  In fact, given the lower than expected production, we have increased our forecast of the deficit from 371,000 tonnes to 471,000 tonnes. 

As has consistently been the case in recent years, the main supporting factor will be lack of supply rather than a surge in demand. Last year, consumption within the mature economies grew by 10.1%.  However, Thomson Reuters GFMS view this as a one-off reaction to the three previous years of sharp decline, when consumption within this category fell by 4.2% (2007), 7.6% (2008) and 18.5% (2009). Somewhat unusually the mature economies provided the bulk of the growth last year due to the cyclical and restocking features mentioned above and in Chapter 3 of this report. However, Thomson Reuters GFMS expects that the BRICs and the other emerging economies will return to be the key drivers of global copper demand. We project that global copper demand in 2014 will be 22.554 million tonnes, which represents a 16.9% improvement on 2010. Apart from external factors such as the dollar and the influence of investment funds, the other key determinant of the market is the level of production. So far the supply response to the record high prices has been limited. Thomson Reuters GFMS estimate that global refined output increased by 4.4% last year, with much of the increase coming from the secondary sector. With regards to scrap, tighter regulations are being introduced for scrap imports into the country and authorities have made their intention to enforce these, as well as any existing ones, clear over the last 18 months. Elsewhere, with the exception of process scrap, which after all is often part of a “closed loop”, we do not expect to see a big wave of recycling from old finished goods before the end of the forecast period. As such, under our Base Case, we do not see scrap availability in China increasing massively over the next few years. In line with the above, Thomson Reuters GFMS expect a deceleration in Chinese refined production growth over the forecast period. For 2011, we expect output to grow by 12.6%. This will be followed by growth of 6.8% in 2012, before easing to 5% in 2013 and just 3% in the final year, by which time output should have reached 5.95 million tonnes. In Japan, we expect production to slip by 6.4% this year as a result of lost output due to smelters being affected by the March 11 earthquake and tsunami. This will be followed by a sharp rebound next year as smelters recover this year’s losses, before growth eases over the final two years. We forecast output to grow by 3.8% over 2011-2014. In India, production growth should accelerate. In line with increasing capacity, notably at Hindalco’s Dahej and Vedanta’s Tuticorim smelters, we expect output in India to grow by 4.1% over the forecast period. Production in Kazakhstan fell 6.6% in 2010, largely reflecting lower output from Kazakhmys’ Balkhash smelter, which in turn resulted from less concentrate supply. Going forward, we are projecting accelerating growth. Capacity in the country will be boosted by the launch of Kazzinc’s 70,000 tonne per year production facility at the Ust-Kamenogorsk metals complex and the start-up of the Benkala SX-EW operation this year, along with increases at Kazakhmys’ Zhezkazgan and Balkhash smelters.
